metadata.title: Gino: Knife Throw, Inside the Godot Code
metadata.audience: makers following the channel's Claude + Walker game workflows
metadata.note: godot-gamedev walker film. Code panels are Godot editor reconstructions with verbatim source; each is followed by real engine output of the same build. No game change, no paid calls, no upload. Vertical companion: designed beats re-rendered as native 9:16 cards or 916 compositions; gameplay re-cut in portrait from the same frames.

beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Liam, in for Bear. That's the kind of prompt Walker expects, reconstructed here, not a transcript. This time we open the project itself: a piece of code, then the exact thing it does on screen, in the real build.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about a 2D action platformer — guide Gino home through three hostile valleys with a sword combo, three throwing knives and three hearts — into a playable Godot project.
props.runningText: illustrative reconstruction — not the historical prompt
output: Built: 6 thin scenes, 14 scripts and a shader, 2,620 lines.
Art from the Unity folder; levels and sound authored.

beats.narration_text: Gino: Knife Throw is built in code. Its six scene files are a few lines each, and twenty-six hundred lines of GDScript build every tile, enemy and menu at runtime, from text maps. So every piece of code we read has a result you can watch.

props.text:
Gino: Knife Throw
is built from scenes.
Text maps build every level.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant writer: text is typed on screen over the narration, so mid-beat samples legitimately show a partial page. The finished text fills the safe area and holds for the last 1.5 s.

beats.narration_text: Open a level scene and there's one node. Run it for eight seconds, and level dot g d has built the rest: a background layer, a world holding the tile map, the rock colliders, sixty-one prop sprites, thirteen pickups, Gino and five enemies, a camera, and two canvas layers for the HUD and the menus. Two hundred nodes.

beats.narration_text: The level script reads the map one tile at a time. A P becomes Gino, with his signals wired to the HUD. A b, w or p becomes a bat, a walker or a plant, standing on that tile, and the level counts it. Diamonds, daggers, hearts, the door and the hint crystals come from letters too.

beats.narration_text: Running eases toward a target speed, faster on the ground than in the air. Gino jumps only when a recent press and a recent floor overlap: that's the buffer and the coyote time. Let go of Space early and it cuts the jump to under half. Then gravity, capped at a maximum fall.

beats.narration_text: Space held the whole way: the full jump, long enough to clear the walker waiting below. The driver chose that jump; the physics are the game's.

beats.narration_text: The combo advances only when a swing finishes. If J was queued during it, the combo is under four, and Gino is on the ground, the next swing starts. Otherwise Gino goes back to normal and the count resets.

beats.narration_text: Each swing is a row: the first and last animation frame that can hit, a reach box relative to Gino's feet, and the damage. Twenty for the first three swings and the jump attack, forty for the magic blast. A hit is recorded per swing, so one swing can't hit the same enemy twice.

beats.narration_text: A knife moves in four small steps every frame, so it can't skip through a thin enemy. Each step checks every enemy: a touch deals thirty and breaks the knife. Then it checks rock at the tip. And it expires after one point three seconds, or off the edge of the level.

beats.narration_text: Outside an attack, the walker turns to face Gino. It chases while he's within its range box, but only if it can walk: there has to be floor ahead and no wall. And when Gino enters the cone in front of it, the bite starts.

beats.narration_text: A hit is ignored while Gino is dead, at a door, or still invulnerable. Otherwise he loses the damage, flashes, and the screen shakes. At zero, he dies. If not, he's hurt for a third of a second, invulnerable for a little over one, and knocked away from whatever hit him.

beats.narration_text: Entering the door works only in play. It hides the prompt, walks Gino in, waits under a second, then completes the level: it records the run, pauses the tree, and fills the panel with score, diamonds, enemies, knives and time.

beats.narration_text: There's no input map in the project settings. The GameState autoload builds it at startup: A and D or the arrows, Space, J or X to slash, K or C to throw. Then the gamepad: A jumps and confirms, Start pauses, and the left stick runs.

beats.narration_text: Here's the defect. Pause toggles the menu and marks the event handled. Restart does the same, but restart reloads the level first. By the next line, this node has left the tree, its viewport is null, and the call fails.

beats.narration_text: Escape, then R. On screen, the level simply restarts. In the log: script error, cannot call set input as handled on a null value, line seven sixty-one.

beats.narration_text: The rest of the project, in one pass. A main menu with Continue and a sound button, a How to Play page, and credits that roll and fade. An audio autoload with sounds and music loops, all synthesized by a Python tool. A level tool that checks every map and simulates the jumps. And a playtest that steers through a hook in the player script. The film's captures pressed the keys instead.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. This is a project you can read top to bottom: thin scenes, levels as text, enemies in under a hundred lines each. Two defects: R on a menu logs a script error, one line too late, and level three's bridge stops a tile short. Its own test steers through a hook; the captures pressed keys. And nobody has played it yet.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude in your own Godot project: Use Walker on my Godot project. Find one handler that changes the scene and then keeps running code. Predict what that code will touch after the node has left the tree. Then write a capture that triggers it with real input and checks the log, and only after that, propose the smallest fix. Liam, in for Bear.
